newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Architect of Slovenia success bids for second run.
newsitem.headline: Architect of Slovenia success bids for second run.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek, called on Monday to form a new government, won credit for anchoring democracy and a thriving economy as prime minister in four of the five years since Slovenia seceded from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Drnovsek, 46, an economist and divorced father of one son, honed his political skills as the penultimate president of former Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1990.
The experience served him well as he needed to perform a delicate balancing act during his term of power in Slovenia to keep a fragile left-right coalition from splitting apart.
He spurned pressure from his own centre-left Liberal Democrat Party last May to jettison the increasingly fractious Christian Democrats from the coalition.
Drnovsek said he intended to keep the government together in the national interest rather than pander to party politics.
His style drew praise from abroad and was a factor in consolidating a smooth transition from communist rule and a command economy, while other ex-Yugoslav republics turned to the gun.
Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats increased their share of the vote in a November 10 general election and remained the biggest party, winning 25 out of 90 parliamentary seats.
But an alliance of three right-wing parties just missed clinching an absolute parliamentary majority by just one seat, boosting their bid to form the new government.

The softly-spoken Drnovesk will have to use all his powers of persuasion to prise one or two of the rightist parties from the alliance to join his administration. Otherwise, Drnovsek has no chance of returning to power.
Despite his success in making Slovenia one of the best performing economies among Europe's ex-communist states, he could not prevent an economic slowdown in 1996.
Current indicators show GDP growth will slow to 3.5 percent in 1996 down from 3.9 percent in 1995.
The government has blamed a decline in growth among EU states, Slovenia's major trading partners, which account for about 70 percent of Slovenia's foreign trade.
Drnovsek has pledged to speed up privatisation, streamline the economy by cutting welfare payments and control inflation, which rose to 8.8 percent in 1996 from 8.6 percent a year ago.

Drnovsek crowned his four years as leader by securing an association agreement with the European Union after patching up a row with Italy over the right of ethnic Italians to reclaim property they fled from at the end of World War Two.
A committed pro-European, Drnovsek predicts that Slovenia should become the first ex-Yugoslav republic to join the EU, possibly by the year 2001.

Slovenia's stability so near to the unpredictable Balkan region has made it a serious contender for NATO membership. Drnovsek says entry into the EU and NATO will remain his priority if he heads the next government.
